claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5–5 wt% graphene nanoplatelets to a W–Cu composite will increase its effective thermal conductivity.
A graphene-modified W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to an otherwise comparable graphene-free W–Cu composite.
A graphene-modified W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to an otherwise comparable graphene-free W–Cu composite.
Heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications expose W–Cu composites to high thermal flux, high temperature, and neutron irradiation.
Well-dispersed graphene nanoplatelets form additional thermal bridges within the W–Cu matrix.
Graphene nanoplatelets have high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Graphene nanoplatelets create efficient heat-transfer pathways in the W–Cu composite.
Graphene nanoplatelets possess robust mechanical properties.
Graphene nanoplatelets possess irradiation resistance relevant to the stated operating environment.
The mechanical properties and irradiation resistance of graphene nanoplatelets help preserve the integrity of the tungsten–copper interface.
Preservation of the tungsten–copper interface allows improved thermal conduction without compromising mechanical durability or irradiation performance.
The graphene-enhanced composite will have approximately 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than the graphene-free baseline.
The proposed benefit depends on keeping graphene loading within approximately 0.5–5 wt% and achieving good dispersion.
Excess graphene loading may cause agglomeration.
Graphene agglomeration may reduce the anticipated thermal-conductivity enhancement.
Graphene agglomeration may adversely affect the composite's mechanical properties.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement depends on graphene dispersion quality and interfacial bonding.
Performance under extreme irradiation depends on graphene dispersion quality and interfacial bonding.
